boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Petersburg record (June 15-18, 1864) in the Richmond-Petersburg Campaign [June 1864-March 1865]. The June 9 attempt (VA098) is a separate record, and the Jerusalem Plank Road record (VA065) begins on June 21; the Bermuda Hundred line fighting of June 16-17 is context. Army-wide returns, raid-wide and multi-action loss totals, and the siege as a whole are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen and live force fields read 104,000 (US 62,000; CS 42,000); the frozen description gives 5,400 defenders on June 15. Humphreys gives Smith 10,000 infantry with Kautz's 2,400 cavalry and 3,700 of Hinks's division; the defenders as Wise's brigade, 2,400 strong, the militia and Dearing's cavalry; the Second Corps as 20,000 enlisted men; Johnson's division as 3,500 without Gracie's brigade of about 1,000; and Beauregard's infantry early on June 16 as probably about 14,000, reinforced by Kershaw and Field on the 18th and later Hill.
claims.rationale: The frozen totals do not state their date or population; Humphreys' figures are for different days and formations, several his own estimates. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Humphreys says Smith, having heard Lee's army was crossing, held what he had on June 15 rather than advance; that an immediate advance would probably have taken Petersburg; that he could not learn why Hancock was not ordered to march at daylight; that Beauregard decided to strip his Bermuda Hundred lines; that Meade fixed the hour of the June 18 attacks himself; and that Grant said all had been done that could be done. Meade says he ordered the June 16 assault by Hancock and Burnside. The frozen commanders are Grant and Meade (US) and Lee and Beauregard (CS); the live page lists Grant and 'Major General Robert Lee'.
claims.rationale: Direction and criticism are attributed as the sources give them; Humphreys' counterfactual is his judgment. The live rank is not adopted. No listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory. Humphreys says a mile and a half of intrenchments with sixteen guns were taken on June 15 and that the positions gained on June 18 remained substantially the lines to the war's end; Meade says the June 18 assaults failed and offensive operations then ceased.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. Ground gained and the failure to take the city are both retained; the siege that followed is context.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 11,386 (US 8,150; CS 3,236) and the live field 7,674 (US 2,974; CS 4,700). Humphreys derives 8,150 Union killed and wounded from the Medical Director's 6,210 wounded, an estimated 1,240 killed and probably 700 for the Eighteenth Corps; with 1,814 missing that gives 9,964, against the Tabular Statement's 10,586. He found no official statement of Confederate losses; Hinks reported 507 killed and wounded in his division.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Humphreys' 8,150 is his estimate with an assumed proportion of killed and matches the frozen Union figure; the frozen and live Confederate figures differ.

open_questions: Hancock's, Smith's, Burnside's and Warren's reports for June 15-18, Beauregard's report and telegrams, Lee's June 16-17 dispatches (read, not selected), the compiled returns (No. 7) and the Medical Director's report remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Humphreys' The Virginia Campaign of ’64 and ’65 (1883) is an interested history by the Army of the Potomac's chief of staff, later commander of its Second Corps, in the same author family as the registered From Gettysburg to the Rapidan; it relies on Meade's, Hancock's, Warren's, Burnside's, Parke's and Wilson's reports and quotes Lee's, Beauregard's and Gordon's despatches, so it is not independent of those families. Gillmore's, Meade's, Hancock's, Burnside's, Wilson's, Hampton's, Stannard's and Lee's papers, printed in Official Records Series I, Volumes XXXVI (Part 2), XL, XLII and XLVI (Part 1), are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; each volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Lee's telegrams largely relay subordinates' reports. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
